Water Retention Value (WRV)\nThe WRV was determined with 0.5 g samples (o.d.) according to ISO 23714.\n(m1 −m2) WRV(%) = × 100% (1)\nm2\nwhere m1 is the weight of the sample after centrifugation and m2 is the weight of the oven-dried sample.\n\n2.4. XRD Analysis\nThe crystallinity of pretreated ﬁbers was determined by a Shimadzu XRD 7000S (Shimadzu,\nKyoto, Japan), while using Cu-Ka radiation. The samples were scanned at 40 kV and 30 mA in a 2θ\nrange of 4–40◦at 1◦/min. It is well known that two polymorphs, cellulose Iα and Iβ, are present in\nnative cellulose; for clarity, all of the reﬂections indexed here are on the Iβ lattice. Before analysis,\nthe experimental data is nine point smoothed with Savitzky–Golay algorithm. The two types of CI\nvalues were obtained from peak intensity method (CI −XI) and peak ﬁtting (CI-XA), respectively.\nThe CI −XI was calculated as in Equation (2) [19].\n(I200 −Iam) CI −XI = × 100% (2)\nI200\nwhere I200 is the maximum diﬀraction intensity value of the (200) lattice plane between the scattering\nangles of 2θ = 22◦and 23◦, and Iam is the minimum diﬀraction intensity of amorphous fraction between\n2θ = 18◦and 19◦.\nAll of the XRD diﬀractograms were smoothed with the Savitzky–Golay algorithm and\nbaseline-corrected with linear ﬁt function. Subsequently, the baseline-corrected diﬀractograms\nwere deconvoluted with the Pearson VII function. The value of the CI-XA equals the area percentage\noccupied by crystalline peaks over the total area of the diﬀraction pattern [20]. In addition, the crystallite\nsize was calculated by the widely used Scherrer Equation (3) [21]:\nk × λ\nL = (3)\n(β × cos θ)\nwhere L is the size that is perpendicular to the lattice plane, k is a constant that depends on the crystal\nshape (0.89), λ is the wavelength of the incident beam in the diﬀraction experiment (0.154 nm), β is the\nfull width at half maximum of the diﬀraction peak, and θ is the Bragg’s angle. In general, the values of\nthe calculated crystallite sizes might be lower than that of the real crystallite sizes, because the peak\nbroadening from the instrumental factors was not considered [22].\n\n2.5. FT-IR Analysis\nTHE FT-IR spectra were recorded on solid samples in KBr pellets by means of an FT-IR Bruker\nVertex 70 spectrometer (Karlsruhe, Germany). Unreﬁned and reﬁned ﬁbers were smashed into powder\nbetween 40 and 60 mesh. Subsequently, the powder sample of each species (5 mg) was dispersed in a\nmatrix of highly pure KBr (500 mg). The spectral was recorded by averaging 64 recordings and at a\nresolution of 4 cm−1 with transmission mode from 4000 cm−1 to 400 cm−1. The results were made on\nthe average spectrum that was obtained from ﬁve recordings.\nThe energy of the H-bonding EH for several OH stretching bands was calculated while using\nEquation (4) [13].\nνo −ν\nEH = (4)\nνo\nνo is the wavenumber corresponding to free OH groups (3650 cm−1), ν is the frequency (cm−1) of\nthe bonded OH groups, and k is a constant (1/k = 2.625 × 102 kJ).",
      "Figure 2. The beating degree and Water Retention Value (WRV) for the unreﬁned and reﬁned samples:\n(a) softwood ﬁbers and (b) hardwood ﬁbers.\nIn Figure 3, the tensile index, zero-span tensile index, and wet-web strength represented as a\nfunction of the reﬁning revolutions. The increment of tensile strength is mainly caused by the increasing\nﬁbrillation and ﬁnes during PFI reﬁning, as mentioned above. The wet–web strength of softwood\nﬁber had a more signiﬁcant increase when compared to that of hardwood ﬁber. It is for that ﬁber\nlength plays an essential role in wet–web strength. The zero-span tensile index was usually used in\ncharacterizing the tensile strength of ﬁbers. The results of the zero-span tensile index showed that\nPFI reﬁning did not reduce ﬁber strength, which is consistent with the report of Kouko et al. [24].\nThe above results showed that PFI reﬁning improved the extent of ﬁbrillation (especially the internal\nﬁbrillation), the swelling of ﬁbers, and the tensile strength of sheets without a decrease of the tensile\nstrength of ﬁbers.\n\nFigure 3. The rheological analysis of wet sheets, the tensile strength of dry sheets, and the ﬁber strength\nfor unreﬁned and reﬁned samples: (a) softwood ﬁbers and (b) hardwood ﬁbers.\n\n3.2. Eﬀect of PFI Reﬁning on Crystalline Index and Crystallite Size\nThe cellulose polymorph of these two ﬁbers had no change during PFI treatment, which illustrates\nthat the PFI reﬁning is a relatively mild mechanical treatment, as the results of XRD in Online Resource\n(Figures S1 and S2) show. In general, the CI-XI and the CI-XA of softwood ﬁbers showed a reduction\nof 4.66% and 15.47%, respectively, and those of hardwood ﬁbers decreased by 2.65% and 19.4%,\nrespectively, as can be seen in Figure 4 and Table 1. The value of the CI-XI was remarkably higher than\nthe CI-XA, which might be caused by the over-ﬁtting of amorphous contribution in the analysis of\nCI-XA. However, the CI-XI and the CI-XA were correlated signiﬁcantly for both softwood ﬁbers and\nhardwood ﬁbers, with a correlation coeﬃcient of 0.919 (p < 0.05) for softwood ﬁbers and 0.925 (p < 0.05)\nfor hardwood ﬁbers, respectively, which is consistent with the report of Ahvenainen et al. [25].",
      "3. Results and Discussions\n\n3.1. The Morphological Analysis, Swelling, and Mechanical Properties\nFor softwood ﬁbers and hardwood ﬁbers, the macro-ﬁbrillation index and the ﬁber length had\na downward trend, and the ﬁnes content has an upward trend for the softwood ﬁbers during PFI\nreﬁning, as can be seen in Figure 1. The macro-ﬁbrillation index and ﬁber length of softwood ﬁbers\nchanged signiﬁcantly. However, two parameters of hardwood ﬁbers had no signiﬁcant variations\nrelative to softwood ﬁbers. It might be because of the lower reﬁning pressure that was applied in\nhardwood ﬁbers. The macro-ﬁbrillation index characterizes external macro-ﬁbrillation. The results of\nﬁber morphology analysis showed that external ﬁbrillation increased with the reﬁning process. It is\nconsistent with the increasing speciﬁc surface area (as shown in Table S1 in Online Resource).\n\nFigure 1. The morphological analysis for the unreﬁned and reﬁned samples: (a) softwood ﬁbers and\n(b) hardwood ﬁbers.\nThe beating degree and the WRV had a signiﬁcant increment with increasing PFI reﬁning\nrevolutions, as can be seen in Figure 2. It is caused by the higher ﬁbrillation that produces the\nnew surface and more pores (as shown in Table S1 in Online Resource). The increase in swelling\ncharacterized by WRV makes the ﬁbers more compliant in transverse [1], which contributes to\nimproving the inter-ﬁber bonding strength of the ﬁber network. The results of ﬁber morphology\nanalysis and water retention value showing that the ﬁbrillation and the separation between ﬁbrils\nincrease with the reﬁning process.",
      "27. Kubicki, J.D.; Yang, H.; Sawada, D.; O’Neill, H.; Oehme, D.; Cosgrove, D. The shape of native plant cellulose\nmicroﬁbrils. Sci. Rep. 2018, 8, 13983. [CrossRef]\n\n28. Yang, H.; Kubicki, J.D. A density functional theory study on the shape of the primary cellulose microﬁbril in\nplants: Eﬀects of C6 exocyclic group conformation and H-bonding. Cellulose 2020, 27, 2389–2402. [CrossRef]\n\n29. Duchemin, B.; Thuault, A.; Vicente, A.; Rigaud, B.; Fernandez, C.; Eve, S. Ultrastructure of cellulose crystallites\nin ﬂax textile ﬁbres. Cellulose 2012, 19, 1837–1854. [CrossRef]",
      "Keywords: natural cellulosic ﬁbers; mechanical reﬁning; Crystallinity; Crystallite size;\nHydrogen bonds\n\n1. Introduction\nMechanical, chemical, and biological treatments are usually adopted to obtain the desired\nphysical and mechanical properties and for further utilization of the natural cellulosic ﬁbers. Therein,\nPapirindustriens forskningsinstitut (PFI) reﬁning is the most common laboratory reﬁner in order to\nimprove the inter-ﬁber bonding capacity [1] and accessibility [2,3], and manufacture the micro-ﬁbrillated\nor nano-ﬁbrillated cellulose [4–6]. The main eﬀects of PFI reﬁning on ﬁbers are: (i) internal\nﬁbrillation—delaminating, loosening, and swelling of ﬁber wall; (ii) external ﬁbrillation—peeling of\nﬁbrils from the ﬁber surface while remaining attached; (iii) ﬁber shortening—ﬁber cutting due to\nshearing action, and (iv) ﬁnes formation—primary ﬁnes come from ray cells and parenchyma cells\nand microﬁbrils that are caused by ﬁber shortening or external ﬁbrillation. Moreover, the PFI reﬁning\ncould be adopted to obtain a higher internal ﬁbrillation than other laboratory reﬁners [1]. These eﬀects\nof the PFI reﬁning on cellulosic ﬁbers will improve the accessibility, the swelling, the ﬂexibility, and the\ninter-ﬁber bonding capacity of ﬁbers. It is assumed that these changes in the macro-level structure and\nproperties are related to the changes of crystallinity and H-bonding network during reﬁning [7,8].\n\nThere are some diﬀerent conclusions regarding to the eﬀects of PFI reﬁning on crystallinity of\ncellulose, not like that of ball milling, which eﬀectively reduces the crystallinity as the treatment\nprogresses. Although some researchers considered that the crystallinity decreased during PFI reﬁning\nfor corn stover [9] or softwood pulp [10], some researchers reported that the crystallinity increased\nPolymers 2020, 12, 2912; doi:10.3390/polym12122912 www.mdpi.com/journal/polymers"
    ]
  }
}

      "[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 3. Results and Discussions > 3.3. It decreased by 7.72% from 28.23% to 26.05% as refining from 0r to 4000 r and then increased by 9.14% from 4000 r to 8000 r, followed by a decrease of 17.13%, with the revolutions increasing from 8000 r to 16,000 r. Regarding the O(6)H···O(3′) H-bonds of hardwood fiber, the trend was almost similar to that of softwood fibers, except for a small increase of 0.45% from 8000 r to 12,000 r (in Table 2b). On the whole, the amount of the O(6)H···O(3′) H-bonds for softwood fibers and hardwood fibers decreased by 16.54% and 5.91% altogether, respectively. The decrease might be due to the cleavage among cellulose molecular chains under the mechanical action of PFI refining, which was closely related to internal and external fibrillation (as seen in Section 3.1). On the other hand, the increase illustrates that there was not only the breakage, but also the formation of O(6)H···O(3′) H-bonds."

WRV采用0.5 g（o.d.）样品并按照ISO 23714测定。 [1]
WRV按公式 WRV(%)=((m1−m2)/m2)×100% 计算。 [1]
公式中m1是离心后样品的质量，m2是烘干后样品的质量。 [1]

PFI2-007 · CI-XI与CI-XA有什么区别？请给出本文CI-XI的公式，并说明CI-XA依据什么计算。

参考答案与评分要点

CI-XI用衍射峰强度计算：(I200−Iam)/I200×100%。CI-XA用晶区峰面积占总衍射面积的百分比计算，来自峰拟合。两者采用不同口径。

表格行检索＋关联补全 · 要点 2.5/3；边界 2/2

CI-XI通过比较XRD峰强度获得，CI-XA通过比较XRD峰面积获得。 [1]
本文中CI-XI采用峰强度法（peak intensity method），CI-XA采用峰拟合（peak fitting）获得。 [3]
本文CI-XI的计算公式为 CI-XI=(I200−Iam)/I200×100%。 [3]
公式中I200是2θ=22°至23°之间(200)晶面的最大衍射强度，Iam是2θ=18°至19°之间无定形部分的最小衍射强度。 [3]
CI-XA等于晶峰面积占整个衍射图总面积的百分比，是在基线校正后用Pearson VII函数对衍射图去卷积计算得到。 [3]
CI-XI值显著高于CI-XA，可能是因为CI-XA分析中无定形贡献存在过拟合。 [2]

  "answer": "CI-XI通过比较XRD峰强度获得，CI-XA通过比较XRD峰面积获得。 [1]\n本文中CI-XI采用峰强度法（peak intensity method），CI-XA采用峰拟合（peak fitting）获得。 [3]\n本文CI-XI的计算公式为 CI-XI=(I200−Iam)/I200×100%。 [3]\n公式中I200是2θ=22°至23°之间(200)晶面的最大衍射强度，Iam是2θ=18°至19°之间无定形部分的最小衍射强度。 [3]\nCI-XA等于晶峰面积占整个衍射图总面积的百分比，是在基线校正后用Pearson VII函数对衍射图去卷积计算得到。 [3]\nCI-XI值显著高于CI-XA，可能是因为CI-XA分析中无定形贡献存在过拟合。 [2]",

      "[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 3. Results and Discussions > 3.3. Efect of PFI Refining on H-Bonding Energies, H-Bonding Distances, and Content of H-Bonds\n[原文]\nAs to the free OH(2) and OH(6) of softwood fiber, the relative content showed a slight increase trend in general. The enhancement of the free OH(2) and OH(6) was understandable, because there was the breakage of H-bonds among cellulosic molecules, which resulted in more extensive delamination and higher specific surface area (as shown in Figure S4 and Table S1 in Online Resource). This made cellulose more accessible to water and chemicals. However, for the free OH(2) and OH(6) of hardwood fiber, the number of the free OH(2) and OH(6) decreased by 21.65% from 14.32% to 11.22%, with revolutions increasing from 0 r to 4000 r, followed by an increase of 45.37% in the stage of refining from 4000 r to 12,000 r, along with an decrease of 17.11%. It could be explained by the instability of free OH groups, which makes it easy to form new H-bonds, such as O(2)H···O(6) or O(6)H···O(3′)H-bonds. Thus although there is the formation of free OH(2) and OH(6) during fibrillation, the content of the free OH(2) and OH(6) might disease; meanwhile, the content of the O(6)H···O(3′) or the O(2)H···O(6) H-bonds might increase upon drying.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 3. Results and Discussions > 3.4. Correlation between CI and Content of Inter-Molecular H-Bonds during PFI Refining\n[原文]\nSimilar to the CI-XI, the content of O(6)H···O(3′) H-bonds decreased first and then had an increase, followed by a decline for the two fibers (as shown in Figure 8a,b). Besides, the Pearson correlation coefficients were calculated between the content of H-bonds and the CI-XI. It was 0.912 (p < 0.05) for softwood fibers and 0.889 (p < 0.05) for hardwood fibers, respectively. The similar trends in the content of the O(6)H···O(3′) H-bonds and the CI-XI might be because that the crystalline region has a higher content of O(6)H···O(3′) H-bonds when compared with the amorphous regions, as illustrated in Figure 9 [35]."
    ]
  }
}
解析修复95块 · 要点 2.5/3；边界 2/2

CI-XI是通过比较XRD峰强度得到的结晶度指数，CI-XA是通过比较XRD峰面积得到的结晶度指数。 [1]
本文CI-XI的计算公式为CI-XI=((I200−Iam)/I200)×100%。 [3]
式中I200是2θ=22°–23°之间(200)晶面的最大衍射强度，Iam是2θ=18°–19°之间非晶部分的最小衍射强度。 [3]
CI-XA等于 crystalline peaks 占整个衍射图谱总面积的面积百分比，其分析采用峰拟合方法。 [3]
CI-XI的值通常显著高于CI-XA，这可能是由于CI-XA分析中对非晶贡献的过拟合造成的。 [2]

Effect of PFI Refining on Crystalline Index and Crystallite Size\n[原文]\nThe cellulose polymorph of these two fibers had no change during PFI treatment, which illustrates that the PFI refining is a relatively mild mechanical treatment, as the results of XRD in Online Resource (Figures S1 and S2) show. In general, the CI-XI and the CI-XA of softwood fibers showed a reduction of 4.66% and 15.47%, respectively, and those of hardwood fibers decreased by 2.65% and 19.4%, respectively, as can be seen in Figure 4 and Table 1. The value of the CI-XI was remarkably higher than the CI-XA, which might be caused by the over-fitting of amorphous contribution in the analysis of CI-XA. However, the CI-XI and the CI-XA were correlated significantly for both softwood fibers and hardwood fibers, with a correlation coefficient of 0.919 (p < 0.05) for softwood fibers and 0.925 (p < 0.05) for hardwood fibers, respectively, which is consistent with the report of Ahvenainen et al. Efect of PFI Refining on H-Bonding Energies, H-Bonding Distances, and Content of H-Bonds\n[原文]\nAs to the free OH(2) and OH(6) of softwood fiber, the relative content showed a slight increase trend in general. The enhancement of the free OH(2) and OH(6) was understandable, because there was the breakage of H-bonds among cellulosic molecules, which resulted in more extensive delamination and higher specific surface area (as shown in Figure S4 and Table S1 in Online Resource). This made cellulose more accessible to water and chemicals. However, for the free OH(2) and OH(6) of hardwood fiber, the number of the free OH(2) and OH(6) decreased by 21.65% from 14.32% to 11.22%, with revolutions increasing from 0 r to 4000 r, followed by an increase of 45.37% in the stage of refining from 4000 r to 12,000 r, along with an decrease of 17.11%. It could be explained by the instability of free OH groups, which makes it easy to form new H-bonds, such as O(2)H···O(6) or O(6)H···O(3′)H-bonds. Thus although there is the formation of free OH(2) and OH(6) during fibrillation, the content of the free OH(2) and OH(6) might disease; meanwhile, the content of the O(6)H···O(3′) or the O(2)H···O(6) H-bonds might increase upon drying.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 3. Results and Discussions > 3.4. Correlation between CI and Content of Inter-Molecular H-Bonds during PFI Refining\n[原文]\nSimilar to the CI-XI, the content of O(6)H···O(3′) H-bonds decreased first and then had an increase, followed by a decline for the two fibers (as shown in Figure 8a,b). Besides, the Pearson correlation coefficients were calculated between the content of H-bonds and the CI-XI. It was 0.912 (p < 0.05) for softwood fibers and 0.889 (p < 0.05) for hardwood fibers, respectively. The similar trends in the content of the O(6)H···O(3′) H-bonds and the CI-XI might be because that the crystalline region has a higher content of O(6)H···O(3′) H-bonds when compared with the amorphous regions, as illustrated in Figure 9 [35]."

PyMuPDF结构81块 · 要点 2.5/3；边界 2/2

本文中CI-XI由峰强度法获得，CI-XA由峰拟合获得。 [3]
本文CI-XI的公式为 CI-XI = (I200 − Iam) / I200 × 100%。 [3]
式中I200为2θ=22°–23°之间(200)晶面的最大衍射强度，Iam为2θ=18°–19°之间无定形部分的最小衍射强度。 [3]
CI-XA等于结晶峰面积占整个衍射图总面积的百分比。 [3]
CI-XA是在Savitzky–Golay平滑和线性基线校正后，用Pearson VII函数对基线校正后的衍射图进行解卷积后计算的。 [3]
CI-XI的值明显高于CI-XA，这可能是因为CI-XA分析中对无定形贡献的过度拟合。 [2]
CI-XI与CI-XA仍显著相关，软木纤维的相关系数为0.919（p < 0.05），硬木纤维为0.925（p < 0.05）。 [2]

      "Polymers 2020, 12, 2912 6 of 14\n\nFigure 4. The CI-XI (crystallinity index obtained by comparing intensity of X-ray diﬀractometer (XRD)\npeaks) and CI-XA (crystallinity index obtained by comparing area of XRD peaks) for reﬁned and\nunreﬁned samples: (a) softwood ﬁber and (b) hardwood ﬁber.\n\nTable 1. (a) The CI of softwood ﬁbers through reﬁning. (b) The CI of hardwood ﬁbers through reﬁning.\n(a)\nCI (%) Crystallite Size (nm)\nRevolutions a b CI-XI CI-XA 110 (110) (200)\n0 73.23 40.46 3.2 3.5 4.5\n4000 70.42 37.71 3.1 3.4 4.6\n8000 72.54 39.65 3.2 3.4 4.6\n12,000 70.93 36.22 3.1 3.7 4.7\n16,000 69.82 34.20 3.2 3.5 4.7\n(b)\nCI (%) Crystallite Size (nm)\nRevolutions a b CI-XI CI-XA 110 (110) (200)\n0 75.55 47.16 3.1 3.1 4.5\n4000 73.01 36.26 3.1 3.3 4.7\n8000 75.06 42.35 3.1 3.5 4.8\n12,000 74.57 39.21 2.9 4.0 4.8\n16,000 73.55 38.01 3.0 3.7 4.7\na The CI-XI value was obtained from the ratio of the diﬀraction intensity. b The CI-XA value was obtained from the\nratio of the peak areas.\n\nThe trends of CI (CI-XI and CI-XA) for softwood ﬁbers and hardwood ﬁbers were all similar,\ndecreasing ﬁrst and then increasing, along with a decline, as shown in Figure 4. The ﬂuctuation of the\nCI was probably because of the mechanical action of PFI reﬁning on the diﬀerent regions of cellulose.\nIn the ﬁrst reﬁning stage, the decrease of the CI showed that mechanical treatment may mainly act in\nthe crystalline region. Subsequently, the growth of the CI could be interpreted as greater force acting\non the amorphous region in which cocrystallization might occur upon drying under the mechanical\nand thermal action of PFI reﬁning. The subsequent decrease might be the continuous destruction of\ncrystalline region.\nRecently, researches indicated that plant cell walls commonly contained microﬁbrils with 18\ncellulose chains [26]. Frequently adopted arrangements of the 18 cellulose chains are 234432, 34443,\nand 333333 [27]. Therein, 234432 arrangement was found to be more probable based on calculation [28].\nThus, according to the crystallite sizes (as Table 1 shows) and the unit cell parameters of cellulose\nIβ, there was most likely to be an average of two-ﬁbrils with an arrangement of 234,432 packed\nside-by-side for both softwood ﬁbers and hardwood ﬁbers (as seen in Figure 5, drawn with mercury",
      "Figure 3. The rheological analysis of wet sheets, the tensile strength of dry sheets, and the ﬁber strength\nfor unreﬁned and reﬁned samples: (a) softwood ﬁbers and (b) hardwood ﬁbers.\n\n3.2. Eﬀect of PFI Reﬁning on Crystalline Index and Crystallite Size\nThe cellulose polymorph of these two ﬁbers had no change during PFI treatment, which illustrates\nthat the PFI reﬁning is a relatively mild mechanical treatment, as the results of XRD in Online Resource\n(Figures S1 and S2) show. In general, the CI-XI and the CI-XA of softwood ﬁbers showed a reduction\nof 4.66% and 15.47%, respectively, and those of hardwood ﬁbers decreased by 2.65% and 19.4%,\nrespectively, as can be seen in Figure 4 and Table 1. The value of the CI-XI was remarkably higher than\nthe CI-XA, which might be caused by the over-ﬁtting of amorphous contribution in the analysis of\nCI-XA. However, the CI-XI and the CI-XA were correlated signiﬁcantly for both softwood ﬁbers and\nhardwood ﬁbers, with a correlation coeﬃcient of 0.919 (p < 0.05) for softwood ﬁbers and 0.925 (p < 0.05)\nfor hardwood ﬁbers, respectively, which is consistent with the report of Ahvenainen et al. [25].",
      "2.3. Water Retention Value (WRV)\nThe WRV was determined with 0.5 g samples (o.d.) according to ISO 23714.\n(m1 −m2) WRV(%) = × 100% (1)\nm2\nwhere m1 is the weight of the sample after centrifugation and m2 is the weight of the oven-dried sample.\n\n2.4. XRD Analysis\nThe crystallinity of pretreated ﬁbers was determined by a Shimadzu XRD 7000S (Shimadzu,\nKyoto, Japan), while using Cu-Ka radiation. The samples were scanned at 40 kV and 30 mA in a 2θ\nrange of 4–40◦at 1◦/min. It is well known that two polymorphs, cellulose Iα and Iβ, are present in\nnative cellulose; for clarity, all of the reﬂections indexed here are on the Iβ lattice. Before analysis,\nthe experimental data is nine point smoothed with Savitzky–Golay algorithm. The two types of CI\nvalues were obtained from peak intensity method (CI −XI) and peak ﬁtting (CI-XA), respectively.\nThe CI −XI was calculated as in Equation (2) [19].\n(I200 −Iam) CI −XI = × 100% (2)\nI200\nwhere I200 is the maximum diﬀraction intensity value of the (200) lattice plane between the scattering\nangles of 2θ = 22◦and 23◦, and Iam is the minimum diﬀraction intensity of amorphous fraction between\n2θ = 18◦and 19◦.\nAll of the XRD diﬀractograms were smoothed with the Savitzky–Golay algorithm and\nbaseline-corrected with linear ﬁt function. Subsequently, the baseline-corrected diﬀractograms\nwere deconvoluted with the Pearson VII function. The value of the CI-XA equals the area percentage\noccupied by crystalline peaks over the total area of the diﬀraction pattern [20]. In addition, the crystallite\nsize was calculated by the widely used Scherrer Equation (3) [21]:\nk × λ\nL = (3)\n(β × cos θ)\nwhere L is the size that is perpendicular to the lattice plane, k is a constant that depends on the crystal\nshape (0.89), λ is the wavelength of the incident beam in the diﬀraction experiment (0.154 nm), β is the\nfull width at half maximum of the diﬀraction peak, and θ is the Bragg’s angle. In general, the values of\nthe calculated crystallite sizes might be lower than that of the real crystallite sizes, because the peak\nbroadening from the instrumental factors was not considered [22].\n\n2.5. FT-IR Analysis\nTHE FT-IR spectra were recorded on solid samples in KBr pellets by means of an FT-IR Bruker\nVertex 70 spectrometer (Karlsruhe, Germany). Unreﬁned and reﬁned ﬁbers were smashed into powder\nbetween 40 and 60 mesh. Subsequently, the powder sample of each species (5 mg) was dispersed in a\nmatrix of highly pure KBr (500 mg). The spectral was recorded by averaging 64 recordings and at a\nresolution of 4 cm−1 with transmission mode from 4000 cm−1 to 400 cm−1. The results were made on\nthe average spectrum that was obtained from ﬁve recordings.\nThe energy of the H-bonding EH for several OH stretching bands was calculated while using\nEquation (4) [13].\nνo −ν\nEH = (4)\nνo\nνo is the wavenumber corresponding to free OH groups (3650 cm−1), ν is the frequency (cm−1) of\nthe bonded OH groups, and k is a constant (1/k = 2.625 × 102 kJ).",
      "In the case of the O(2)H· · · O(6) intra-molecular H-bonds for softwood ﬁber, the trend of content\ncan be described as two phases. It had an increase of 3.5% from 31.4% to 32.5% in the stage of reﬁning\nfrom 0 r to 4000 r and it then decreased by 21.57% from 4000 r to 12000 r, along with a growth of 15.26%\nin the last reﬁning stage. For the content of the O(2)H· · · O(6) H-bonds of hardwood ﬁber, it increased\nﬁrstly and then had a decrease that was also followed by an increase. For both ﬁbers, the content of\nO(2)H· · · O(6) H-bonds decreased, except for the stage of reﬁning from 0 r to 4000 r. It might be due to\nthe fact that the O(2)H· · · O(6) H-bonds, which are much more accessible to water, are less stable than\nO(3)H· · · O(5) H-bonds.\nAs to the free OH(2) and OH(6) of softwood fiber, the relative content showed a slight increase trend\nin general. The enhancement of the free OH(2) and OH(6) was understandable, because there was the\nbreakage of H-bonds among cellulosic molecules, which resulted in more extensive delamination and\nhigher specific surface area (as shown in Figure S4 and Table S1 in Online Resource). This made cellulose\nmore accessible to water and chemicals. However, for the free OH(2) and OH(6) of hardwood fiber,\nthe number of the free OH(2) and OH(6) decreased by 21.65% from 14.32% to 11.22%, with revolutions\nincreasing from 0 r to 4000 r, followed by an increase of 45.37% in the stage of refining from 4000 r to\n12,000 r, along with an decrease of 17.11%. It could be explained by the instability of free OH groups,\nwhich makes it easy to form new H-bonds, such as O(2)H···O(6) or O(6)H···O(3′)H-bonds. Thus although\nthere is the formation of free OH(2) and OH(6) during fibrillation, the content of the free OH(2) and OH(6)\nmight disease; meanwhile, the content of the O(6)H···O(3′) or the O(2)H···O(6) H-bonds might increase\nupon drying.\n\n3.4. Correlation between CI and Content of Inter-Molecular H-Bonds during PFI Reﬁning\nSimilar to the CI-XI, the content of O(6)H· · · O(3′) H-bonds decreased ﬁrst and then had an increase,\nfollowed by a decline for the two ﬁbers (as shown in Figure 8a,b). Besides, the Pearson correlation\ncoeﬃcients were calculated between the content of H-bonds and the CI-XI. It was 0.912 (p < 0.05)\nfor softwood ﬁbers and 0.889 (p < 0.05) for hardwood ﬁbers, respectively. The similar trends in the\ncontent of the O(6)H· · · O(3′) H-bonds and the CI-XI might be because that the crystalline region has a\nhigher content of O(6)H· · · O(3′) H-bonds when compared with the amorphous regions, as illustrated\nin Figure 9 [35].",
      "Polymers 2020, 12, 2912 11 of 14\n\nFigure 8. The trend of the CI-XI, the CI-XA, and the O(6)H· · · O(3′) H-bonds: (a) softwood ﬁbers and\n(b) hardwood ﬁbers.\n\nFigure 9. The illustration of a two-phase structure of cellulose.\nThe correlation between the CI-XI and the O(2)H· · · O(6) H-bonds or the free OH(2) and OH(6)\nwas poor for the following reasons. The free OH groups are easier for forming the O(2)H· · · O(6)\nH-bonds as opposed to the O(6)H· · · O(3′) H-bonds in the amorphous region, because the distance\nbetween adjacent glucose units in a cellulosic molecular chain is closer than between the glucose units\nin the adjacent molecular chain (as shown in Figure 9). Accordingly, when compared with the content\nof O(6)H· · · O(3′) H-bonds, there was less diﬀerence in the content of the O(2)H· · · O(6) H-bonds or the\nfree OH groups between the crystalline region and amorphous region, which sometimes made the\ncontent of the two bonds not change much in regards to the crystallinity. The O(3)H· · · O(5) H-bonds\nis stable, as mentioned above. It was presumed to change little as crystallinity changed during PFI\nreﬁning. Hence, the correlation between O(3)H· · · O(5) H-bonds and the CI-XI was not discussed in the\npresent study.\n\n4. Conclusions\nPFI reﬁning acts not only on the macro-level structure and mechanical properties, but also on\nthe supramolecular structure, including crystallite size, crystallinity, and content of various H-bonds."

XRD Analysis\n[原文]\nThe crystallinity of pretreated fibers was determined by a Shimadzu XRD 7000S (Shimadzu, Kyoto, Japan), while using Cu-Ka radiation. The samples were scanned at 40 kV and 30 mA in a 2θ range of $4 { - } 4 0 ^ { \\circ }$ at 1<sup>◦</sup>/min. It is well known that two polymorphs, cellulose Iα and Iβ, are present in native cellulose; for clarity, all of the reflections indexed here are on the Iβ lattice. Before analysis, the experimental data is nine point smoothed with Savitzky–Golay algorithm. The two types of CI values were obtained from peak intensity method (CI − XI) and peak fitting (CI-XA), respectively. The CI − XI was calculated as in Equation (2) [19].\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 2. Methods > 2.4. XRD Analysis\n[原文]\n$$\nC I - X I = \\frac {\\left(I _ {2 0 0} - I _ {a m}\\right)}{I _ {2 0 0}} \\times 1 0 0 \\%\\tag{2}\n$$",
      "[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 1. Introduction\n[原文]\nThere is still a lack of literature on the efects of PFI refinement on the H-bonding network. Particularly, the relationship between the content of H-bonds and crystallinity is still worthy of further study, which will deepen the understanding of the molecular aggregation and distribution of H-bonds, providing a molecular-scale explanation for the variations in accessibility, swelling, flexibility, and fibrillation of cellulosic fibers during PFI refinement. Therefore, this work explored the efects of PFI refinement on the CI, crystallite size, energy of H-bonds, H-bonding distance, and content of H-bonds for softwood pulp fibers and hardwood pulp fibers. Attempts were made in order to establish the correlations between the CI and content of various H-bonds.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 2. Methods > 2.1. PFI Refining\n[原文]\nCommercial bleached softwood and hardwood kraft pulp fibers were obtained from Zhongzhirenhe Company (Jinan, Shandong Province, China). Two pulp were treated with a PFI refiner (Hamjern Maskin A/S, Hamar, Norway) according to Tappi T248 wd-97, with a pulp consistency of 10%, the gap between the opposite refining plates was 0.2 mm, and forces per bar length were 3.33 N/mm and 1.77 N/mm for softwood fibers and hardwood fibers, respectively. The drainability was characterized by the Schopper Riegler number (SR-number) with the standards ISO 5267-1. Two pulp fibers were separately refined in a PFI refiner at 0, 4000, 8000, 12,000, and 16,000 revolutions and at 0, 4000, 8000, 12,000, and 16,000 revolutions, respectively. Corresponding various pulps with an increasing beating degree, such as 16, 20, 40, 63, and 79<sup>◦</sup> SR, were obtained for softwood fibers and 0, 26, 40, 57, and 70<sup>◦</sup> SR were obtained for hardwood fibers.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 2. Methods > 2.2. Morphological Analysis of Fibers and Mechanical Properties of Sheets\n[原文]\nThe fines content, weighted mean length, and macro-fibrillation index of each sample were determined with a MORFI LB analyzer (Techpap SAS, Grenoble, France). The tensile strength of dry sheets and Wet-web strength were tested according to TAPPI T494 and Chinese standard GBT 12914-2008, respectively. The zero-span tensile strength was tested with the Z-Span 2400 apparatus (Pulmac International Co. Ltd., Montpelier, VT, USA), according to the standard ISO 15361.",
      "[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 4. Conclusions\n[原文]\nThe results indicated that the fibrillation and properties of fibers are related to the variation of the supramolecular structure during PFI refining. It is noticeable that there was a significantly positive correlation between the CI-XI and content of O(6)H· · · O(3)’ H-bonds during PFI refining for softwood fibers and hardwood fibers. Thus, the trend of the content of O(6)H· · · O(3)’ H-bonds might be generally speculated based on CI-XI while refining. Besides, the crystallite size, crystallinity, and content of various H-bonds did not change much in general. It is assumed that PFI refining is an excellent mechanical treatment of fibrillation with relatively little destruction on the supramolecular structure.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 4. XRD Analysis\n[原文]\nThe crystallinity of pretreated fibers was determined by a Shimadzu XRD 7000S (Shimadzu, Kyoto, Japan), while using Cu-Ka radiation. The samples were scanned at 40 kV and 30 mA in a 2θ range of $4 { - } 4 0 ^ { \\circ }$ at 1<sup>◦</sup>/min. It is well known that two polymorphs, cellulose Iα and Iβ, are present in native cellulose; for clarity, all of the reflections indexed here are on the Iβ lattice. Before analysis, the experimental data is nine point smoothed with Savitzky–Golay algorithm. The two types of CI values were obtained from peak intensity method (CI − XI) and peak fitting (CI-XA), respectively. The CI − XI was calculated as in Equation (2) [19].\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 2. Methods > 2.4. XRD Analysis\n[原文]\n$$\nC I - X I = \\frac {\\left(I _ {2 0 0} - I _ {a m}\\right)}{I _ {2 0 0}} \\times 1 0 0 \\%\\tag{2}\n$$",
      "[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 1. Introduction\n[原文]\nThere is still a lack of literature on the efects of PFI refinement on the H-bonding network. Particularly, the relationship between the content of H-bonds and crystallinity is still worthy of further study, which will deepen the understanding of the molecular aggregation and distribution of H-bonds, providing a molecular-scale explanation for the variations in accessibility, swelling, flexibility, and fibrillation of cellulosic fibers during PFI refinement. Therefore, this work explored the efects of PFI refinement on the CI, crystallite size, energy of H-bonds, H-bonding distance, and content of H-bonds for softwood pulp fibers and hardwood pulp fibers. Attempts were made in order to establish the correlations between the CI and content of various H-bonds.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 2. Methods > 2.1. PFI Refining\n[原文]\nCommercial bleached softwood and hardwood kraft pulp fibers were obtained from Zhongzhirenhe Company (Jinan, Shandong Province, China). Two pulp were treated with a PFI refiner (Hamjern Maskin A/S, Hamar, Norway) according to Tappi T248 wd-97, with a pulp consistency of 10%, the gap between the opposite refining plates was 0.2 mm, and forces per bar length were 3.33 N/mm and 1.77 N/mm for softwood fibers and hardwood fibers, respectively. The drainability was characterized by the Schopper Riegler number (SR-number) with the standards ISO 5267-1. Two pulp fibers were separately refined in a PFI refiner at 0, 4000, 8000, 12,000, and 16,000 revolutions and at 0, 4000, 8000, 12,000, and 16,000 revolutions, respectively. Corresponding various pulps with an increasing beating degree, such as 16, 20, 40, 63, and 79<sup>◦</sup> SR, were obtained for softwood fibers and 0, 26, 40, 57, and 70<sup>◦</sup> SR were obtained for hardwood fibers.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 2. Methods > 2.2. Morphological Analysis of Fibers and Mechanical Properties of Sheets\n[原文]\nThe fines content, weighted mean length, and macro-fibrillation index of each sample were determined with a MORFI LB analyzer (Techpap SAS, Grenoble, France). The tensile strength of dry sheets and Wet-web strength were tested according to TAPPI T494 and Chinese standard GBT 12914-2008, respectively. The zero-span tensile strength was tested with the Z-Span 2400 apparatus (Pulmac International Co. Ltd., Montpelier, VT, USA), according to the standard ISO 15361.",
      "[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 4. Conclusions\n[原文]\nThe results indicated that the fibrillation and properties of fibers are related to the variation of the supramolecular structure during PFI refining. It is noticeable that there was a significantly positive correlation between the CI-XI and content of O(6)H· · · O(3)’ H-bonds during PFI refining for softwood fibers and hardwood fibers. Thus, the trend of the content of O(6)H· · · O(3)’ H-bonds might be generally speculated based on CI-XI while refining. Besides, the crystallite size, crystallinity, and content of various H-bonds did not change much in general. It is assumed that PFI refining is an excellent mechanical treatment of fibrillation with relatively little destruction on the supramolecular structure.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 4. Conclusions\n[原文]\nSupplementary Materials: The following are available online at http://www.mdpi.com/2073-4360/12/12/2912/s1, Figure S1: XRD fitting results of softwood fibers: (a) 0, (b) 4000, (c) 8000, (d) 12,000, (e) 16,000 revolutions of PFI refining, Figure S2: XRD fitting results of hardwood fibers: (a) 0, (b) 4000, (c) 8000, (d) 12,000, (e) 16,000 revolutions of PFI refining, Figure S3: Nonlinear fitting curves of the band of hardwood fibers for hydroxyl groups: (a) 0, (b) 4000, (c) 8000, (d) 12,000, (e) 16,000 revolutions of PFI refining, Figure S4: The BET N2 adsorption/desorption isotherms at various refining revolutions of pulp fibers: (a) softwood; (b) hardwood, Table S1: Cumulative pore volume, average pore size and specific surface area of softwood pulp fiber through refining, Cumulative pore volume, average pore size and specific surface area of hardwood pulp fiber through refining."

Eﬀect of PFI Reﬁning on Crystalline Index and Crystallite Size\nThe cellulose polymorph of these two ﬁbers had no change during PFI treatment, which illustrates\nthat the PFI reﬁning is a relatively mild mechanical treatment, as the results of XRD in Online Resource\n(Figures S1 and S2) show. In general, the CI-XI and the CI-XA of softwood ﬁbers showed a reduction\nof 4.66% and 15.47%, respectively, and those of hardwood ﬁbers decreased by 2.65% and 19.4%,\nrespectively, as can be seen in Figure 4 and Table 1. [25].",
      "Polymers 2020, 12, 2912 12 of 14\nThe results indicated that the ﬁbrillation and properties of ﬁbers are related to the variation of the\nsupramolecular structure during PFI reﬁning. It is noticeable that there was a signiﬁcantly positive\ncorrelation between the CI-XI and content of O(6)H· · · O(3)’ H-bonds during PFI reﬁning for softwood\nﬁbers and hardwood ﬁbers. Thus, the trend of the content of O(6)H· · · O(3)’ H-bonds might be generally\nspeculated based on CI-XI while reﬁning. Besides, the crystallite size, crystallinity, and content of\nvarious H-bonds did not change much in general. The samples were scanned at 40 kV and 30 mA in a 2θ\nrange of 4–40◦at 1◦/min. It is well known that two polymorphs, cellulose Iα and Iβ, are present in\nnative cellulose; for clarity, all of the reﬂections indexed here are on the Iβ lattice. Before analysis,\nthe experimental data is nine point smoothed with Savitzky–Golay algorithm. The two types of CI\nvalues were obtained from peak intensity method (CI −XI) and peak ﬁtting (CI-XA), respectively.\nThe CI −XI was calculated as in Equation (2) [19].\n(I200 −Iam) CI −XI = × 100% (2)\nI200\nwhere I200 is the maximum diﬀraction intensity value of the (200) lattice plane between the scattering\nangles of 2θ = 22◦and 23◦, and Iam is the minimum diﬀraction intensity of amorphous fraction between\n2θ = 18◦and 19◦.\nAll of the XRD diﬀractograms were smoothed with the Savitzky–Golay algorithm and\nbaseline-corrected with linear ﬁt function. Subsequently, the baseline-corrected diﬀractograms\nwere deconvoluted with the Pearson VII function. The value of the CI-XA equals the area percentage\noccupied by crystalline peaks over the total area of the diﬀraction pattern [20]. In addition, the crystallite\nsize was calculated by the widely used Scherrer Equation (3) [21]:\nk × λ\nL = (3)\n(β × cos θ)\nwhere L is the size that is perpendicular to the lattice plane, k is a constant that depends on the crystal\nshape (0.89), λ is the wavelength of the incident beam in the diﬀraction experiment (0.154 nm), β is the\nfull width at half maximum of the diﬀraction peak, and θ is the Bragg’s angle. In general, the values of\nthe calculated crystallite sizes might be lower than that of the real crystallite sizes, because the peak\nbroadening from the instrumental factors was not considered [22].\n\n2.5. FT-IR Analysis\nTHE FT-IR spectra were recorded on solid samples in KBr pellets by means of an FT-IR Bruker\nVertex 70 spectrometer (Karlsruhe, Germany). Unreﬁned and reﬁned ﬁbers were smashed into powder\nbetween 40 and 60 mesh. Subsequently, the powder sample of each species (5 mg) was dispersed in a\nmatrix of highly pure KBr (500 mg). The spectral was recorded by averaging 64 recordings and at a\nresolution of 4 cm−1 with transmission mode from 4000 cm−1 to 400 cm−1. The results were made on\nthe average spectrum that was obtained from ﬁve recordings.\nThe energy of the H-bonding EH for several OH stretching bands was calculated while using\nEquation (4) [13].\nνo −ν\nEH = (4)\nνo\nνo is the wavenumber corresponding to free OH groups (3650 cm−1), ν is the frequency (cm−1) of\nthe bonded OH groups, and k is a constant (1/k = 2.625 × 102 kJ).",
      "Polymers 2020, 12, 2912 11 of 14\n\nFigure 8. The trend of the CI-XI, the CI-XA, and the O(6)H· · · O(3′) H-bonds: (a) softwood ﬁbers and\n(b) hardwood ﬁbers.\n\nFigure 9. The illustration of a two-phase structure of cellulose.\nThe correlation between the CI-XI and the O(2)H· · · O(6) H-bonds or the free OH(2) and OH(6)\nwas poor for the following reasons. The free OH groups are easier for forming the O(2)H· · · O(6)\nH-bonds as opposed to the O(6)H· · · O(3′) H-bonds in the amorphous region, because the distance\nbetween adjacent glucose units in a cellulosic molecular chain is closer than between the glucose units\nin the adjacent molecular chain (as shown in Figure 9). Accordingly, when compared with the content\nof O(6)H· · · O(3′) H-bonds, there was less diﬀerence in the content of the O(2)H· · · O(6) H-bonds or the\nfree OH groups between the crystalline region and amorphous region, which sometimes made the\ncontent of the two bonds not change much in regards to the crystallinity. The O(3)H· · · O(5) H-bonds\nis stable, as mentioned above. It was presumed to change little as crystallinity changed during PFI\nreﬁning. Hence, the correlation between O(3)H· · · O(5) H-bonds and the CI-XI was not discussed in the\npresent study.",
      "2. Methods\n\n2.1. PFI Reﬁning\nCommercial bleached softwood and hardwood kraft pulp ﬁbers were obtained from\nZhongzhirenhe Company (Jinan, Shandong Province, China). Two pulp were treated with a PFI reﬁner\n(Hamjern Maskin A/S, Hamar, Norway) according to Tappi T248 wd-97, with a pulp consistency\nof 10%, the gap between the opposite reﬁning plates was 0.2 mm, and forces per bar length were\n3.33 N/mm and 1.77 N/mm for softwood ﬁbers and hardwood ﬁbers, respectively. The drainability was\ncharacterized by the Schopper Riegler number (SR-number) with the standards ISO 5267-1. Two pulp\nﬁbers were separately reﬁned in a PFI reﬁner at 0, 4000, 8000, 12,000, and 16,000 revolutions and\nat 0, 4000, 8000, 12,000, and 16,000 revolutions, respectively. Corresponding various pulps with an\nincreasing beating degree, such as 16, 20, 40, 63, and 79◦SR, were obtained for softwood ﬁbers and 0,\n26, 40, 57, and 70◦SR were obtained for hardwood ﬁbers.\n\n2.2. Morphological Analysis of Fibers and Mechanical Properties of Sheets\nThe ﬁnes content, weighted mean length, and macro-ﬁbrillation index of each sample were\ndetermined with a MORFI LB analyzer (Techpap SAS, Grenoble, France). The tensile strength of\ndry sheets and Wet-web strength were tested according to TAPPI T494 and Chinese standard GBT\n12914-2008, respectively. The zero-span tensile strength was tested with the Z-Span 2400 apparatus\n(Pulmac International Co. Ltd., Montpelier, VT, USA), according to the standard ISO 15361."

PFI2-009 · 阔叶木的CI-XA从不打浆到打到8000转降了多少个百分点？相对降了百分之几？把算式写出来。

参考答案与评分要点

阔叶木CI-XA由0转47.16%降到8000转42.35%：绝对差47.16−42.35=4.81个百分点；相对降幅4.81/47.16×100%≈10.20%。论文正文只给出0→16000转的整体降幅19.4%，这里是按表中数值自行计算的中间区间。

Effect of PFI Refining on Crystalline Index and Crystallite Size\n[原文]\nThe trends of CI (CI-XI and CI-XA) for softwood fibers and hardwood fibers were all similar, decreasing first and then increasing, along with a decline, as shown in Figure 4. The fluctuation of the CI was probably because of the mechanical action of PFI refining on the diferent regions of cellulose. In the first refining stage, the decrease of the CI showed that mechanical treatment may mainly act in the crystalline region. Subsequently, the growth of the CI could be interpreted as greater force acting on the amorphous region in which cocrystallization might occur upon drying under the mechanical and thermal action of PFI refining. The subsequent decrease might be the continuous destruction of crystalline region.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 3. Results and Discussions > 3.2. Results and Discussions > 3.2. Effect of PFI Refining on Crystalline Index and Crystallite Size\n[原文]\nThe trends of CI (CI-XI and CI-XA) for softwood fibers and hardwood fibers were all similar, decreasing first and then increasing, along with a decline, as shown in Figure 4. The fluctuation of the CI was probably because of the mechanical action of PFI refining on the diferent regions of cellulose. In the first refining stage, the decrease of the CI showed that mechanical treatment may mainly act in the crystalline region. Subsequently, the growth of the CI could be interpreted as greater force acting on the amorphous region in which cocrystallization might occur upon drying under the mechanical and thermal action of PFI refining. The subsequent decrease might be the continuous destruction of crystalline region.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 3. Results and Discussions > 3.2. Effect of PFI Refining on Crystalline Index and Crystallite Size\n[原文]\nRecently, researches indicated that plant cell walls commonly contained microfibrils with 18 cellulose chains [26]. Frequently adopted arrangements of the 18 cellulose chains are 234432, 34443, and 333333 [27]. Therein, 234432 arrangement was found to be more probable based on calculation [28]. Thus, according to the crystallite sizes (as Table 1 shows) and the unit cell parameters of cellulose Iβ, there was most likely to be an average of two-fibrils with an arrangement of 234,432 packed side-by-side for both softwood fibers and hardwood fibers (as seen in Figure 5, drawn with mercury",

It decreased by 7.72% from 28.23% to 26.05% as refining from 0r to 4000 r and then increased by 9.14% from 4000 r to 8000 r, followed by a decrease of 17.13%, with the revolutions increasing from 8000 r to 16,000 r. Regarding the O(6)H···O(3′) H-bonds of hardwood fiber, the trend was almost similar to that of softwood fibers, except for a small increase of 0.45% from 8000 r to 12,000 r (in Table 2b). On the whole, the amount of the O(6)H···O(3′) H-bonds for softwood fibers and hardwood fibers decreased by 16.54% and 5.91% altogether, respectively. The decrease might be due to the cleavage among cellulose molecular chains under the mechanical action of PFI refining, which was closely related to internal and external fibrillation (as seen in Section 3.1). On the other hand, the increase illustrates that there was not only the breakage, but also the formation of O(6)H···O(3′) H-bonds.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 3. Results and Discussions > 3.3.       "[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 4. Conclusions\n[原文]\nThe results indicated that the fibrillation and properties of fibers are related to the variation of the supramolecular structure during PFI refining. It is noticeable that there was a significantly positive correlation between the CI-XI and content of O(6)H· · · O(3)’ H-bonds during PFI refining for softwood fibers and hardwood fibers. Thus, the trend of the content of O(6)H· · · O(3)’ H-bonds might be generally speculated based on CI-XI while refining. Besides, the crystallite size, crystallinity, and content of various H-bonds did not change much in general. It is assumed that PFI refining is an excellent mechanical treatment of fibrillation with relatively little destruction on the supramolecular structure.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 4. Results and Discussions > 3.2. Effect of PFI Refining on Crystalline Index and Crystallite Size\n[原文]\nThe cellulose polymorph of these two fibers had no change during PFI treatment, which illustrates that the PFI refining is a relatively mild mechanical treatment, as the results of XRD in Online Resource (Figures S1 and S2) show. In general, the CI-XI and the CI-XA of softwood fibers showed a reduction of 4.66% and 15.47%, respectively, and those of hardwood fibers decreased by 2.65% and 19.4%, respectively, as can be seen in Figure 4 and Table 1. The value of the CI-XI was remarkably higher than the CI-XA, which might be caused by the over-fitting of amorphous contribution in the analysis of CI-XA. However, the CI-XI and the CI-XA were correlated significantly for both softwood fibers and hardwood fibers, with a correlation coefficient of 0.919 (p < 0.05) for softwood fibers and 0.925 (p < 0.05) for hardwood fibers, respectively, which is consistent with the report of Ahvenainen et al. Effect of PFI Refining on Crystalline Index and Crystallite Size\n[原文]\nThe trends of CI (CI-XI and CI-XA) for softwood fibers and hardwood fibers were all similar, decreasing first and then increasing, along with a decline, as shown in Figure 4. Subsequently, the growth of the CI could be interpreted as greater force acting on the amorphous region in which cocrystallization might occur upon drying under the mechanical and thermal action of PFI refining. The decrease might be due to the cleavage among cellulose molecular chains under the mechanical action of PFI refining, which was closely related to internal and external fibrillation (as seen in Section 3.1).       "[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 4. Conclusions\n[原文]\nThe results indicated that the fibrillation and properties of fibers are related to the variation of the supramolecular structure during PFI refining. It is noticeable that there was a significantly positive correlation between the CI-XI and content of O(6)H· · · O(3)’ H-bonds during PFI refining for softwood fibers and hardwood fibers. Thus, the trend of the content of O(6)H· · · O(3)’ H-bonds might be generally speculated based on CI-XI while refining. Besides, the crystallite size, crystallinity, and content of various H-bonds did not change much in general. It is assumed that PFI refining is an excellent mechanical treatment of fibrillation with relatively little destruction on the supramolecular structure.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 4. The illustration of a two-phase structure of cellulose.\nThe correlation between the CI-XI and the O(2)H· · · O(6) H-bonds or the free OH(2) and OH(6)\nwas poor for the following reasons. The free OH groups are easier for forming the O(2)H· · · O(6)\nH-bonds as opposed to the O(6)H· · · O(3′) H-bonds in the amorphous region, because the distance\nbetween adjacent glucose units in a cellulosic molecular chain is closer than between the glucose units\nin the adjacent molecular chain (as shown in Figure 9). Accordingly, when compared with the content\nof O(6)H· · · O(3′) H-bonds, there was less diﬀerence in the content of the O(2)H· · · O(6) H-bonds or the\nfree OH groups between the crystalline region and amorphous region, which sometimes made the\ncontent of the two bonds not change much in regards to the crystallinity. The O(3)H· · · O(5) H-bonds\nis stable, as mentioned above. It was presumed to change little as crystallinity changed during PFI\nreﬁning. Hence, the correlation between O(3)H· · · O(5) H-bonds and the CI-XI was not discussed in the\npresent study.",
      "Polymers 2020, 12, 2912 12 of 14\nThe results indicated that the ﬁbrillation and properties of ﬁbers are related to the variation of the\nsupramolecular structure during PFI reﬁning. It is noticeable that there was a signiﬁcantly positive\ncorrelation between the CI-XI and content of O(6)H· · · O(3)’ H-bonds during PFI reﬁning for softwood\nﬁbers and hardwood ﬁbers. Thus, the trend of the content of O(6)H· · · O(3)’ H-bonds might be generally\nspeculated based on CI-XI while reﬁning. Besides, the crystallite size, crystallinity, and content of\nvarious H-bonds did not change much in general. It is assumed that PFI reﬁning is an excellent\nmechanical treatment of ﬁbrillation with relatively little destruction on the supramolecular structure.\nSupplementary Materials: The following are available online at http://www.mdpi.com/2073-4360/12/12/2912/s1,\nFigure S1: XRD ﬁtting results of softwood ﬁbers: (a) 0, (b) 4000, (c) 8000, (d) 12,000, (e) 16,000 revolutions of PFI\nreﬁning, Figure S2: XRD ﬁtting results of hardwood ﬁbers: (a) 0, (b) 4000, (c) 8000, (d) 12,000, (e) 16,000 revolutions\nof PFI reﬁning, Figure S3: Nonlinear ﬁtting curves of the band of hardwood ﬁbers for hydroxyl groups: (a) 0, (b)\n4000, (c) 8000, (d) 12,000, (e) 16,000 revolutions of PFI reﬁning, Figure S4: The BET N2 adsorption/desorption\nisotherms at various reﬁning revolutions of pulp ﬁbers: (a) softwood; (b) hardwood, Table S1: Cumulative pore\nvolume, average pore size and speciﬁc surface area of softwood pulp ﬁber through reﬁning, Cumulative pore\nvolume, average pore size and speciﬁc surface area of hardwood pulp ﬁber through reﬁning.\n\nAuthor Contributions: Conceptualization, methodology, software, validation, formal analysis, investigation,\ndata curation, writing—original draft preparation, and visualization: K.L.; conceptualization, validation, funding\nacquisition, writing—review and editing: L.Z.; conceptualization, resources, supervision, project administration,\nand funding acquisition: B.H.       "[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 1. Introduction\n[原文]\nThere is still a lack of literature on the efects of PFI refinement on the H-bonding network. Particularly, the relationship between the content of H-bonds and crystallinity is still worthy of further study, which will deepen the understanding of the molecular aggregation and distribution of H-bonds, providing a molecular-scale explanation for the variations in accessibility, swelling, flexibility, and fibrillation of cellulosic fibers during PFI refinement. Therefore, this work explored the efects of PFI refinement on the CI, crystallite size, energy of H-bonds, H-bonding distance, and content of H-bonds for softwood pulp fibers and hardwood pulp fibers. Attempts were made in order to establish the correlations between the CI and content of various H-bonds.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 2. Methods > 2.1. PFI Refining\n[原文]\nCommercial bleached softwood and hardwood kraft pulp fibers were obtained from Zhongzhirenhe Company (Jinan, Shandong Province, China). Two pulp were treated with a PFI refiner (Hamjern Maskin A/S, Hamar, Norway) according to Tappi T248 wd-97, with a pulp consistency of 10%, the gap between the opposite refining plates was 0.2 mm, and forces per bar length were 3.33 N/mm and 1.77 N/mm for softwood fibers and hardwood fibers, respectively. The drainability was characterized by the Schopper Riegler number (SR-number) with the standards ISO 5267-1. Two pulp fibers were separately refined in a PFI refiner at 0, 4000, 8000, 12,000, and 16,000 revolutions and at 0, 4000, 8000, 12,000, and 16,000 revolutions, respectively. Corresponding various pulps with an increasing beating degree, such as 16, 20, 40, 63, and 79<sup>◦</sup> SR, were obtained for softwood fibers and 0, 26, 40, 57, and 70<sup>◦</sup> SR were obtained for hardwood fibers.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 2. Methods > 2.2. Morphological Analysis of Fibers and Mechanical Properties of Sheets\n[原文]\nThe fines content, weighted mean length, and macro-fibrillation index of each sample were determined with a MORFI LB analyzer (Techpap SAS, Grenoble, France). The tensile strength of dry sheets and Wet-web strength were tested according to TAPPI T494 and Chinese standard GBT 12914-2008, respectively. The zero-span tensile strength was tested with the Z-Span 2400 apparatus (Pulmac International Co. Ltd., Montpelier, VT, USA), according to the standard ISO 15361.",
      "[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 3. Results and Discussions > 3.1. The Morphological Analysis, Swelling, and Mechanical Properties\n[原文]\nFigure 1. The Morphological Analysis, Swelling, and Mechanical Properties\n[原文]\nThe beating degree and the WRV had a significant increment with increasing PFI refining revolutions, as can be seen in Figure 2. It is caused by the higher fibrillation that produces the new surface and more pores (as shown in Table S1 in Online Resource). The increase in swelling characterized by WRV makes the fibers more compliant in transverse [1], which contributes to improving the inter-fiber bonding strength of the fiber network. The results of fiber morphology analysis and water retention value showing that the fibrillation and the separation between fibrils increase with the refining process.",
      "[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 1. Introduction\n[原文]\nMechanical, chemical, and biological treatments are usually adopted to obtain the desired physical and mechanical properties and for further utilization of the natural cellulosic fibers. Therein, Papirindustriens forskningsinstitut (PFI) refining is the most common laboratory refiner in order to improve the inter-fiber bonding capacity [1] and accessibility [2,3], and manufacture the micro-fibrillated or nano-fibrillated cellulose [4–6]. The main efects of PFI refining on fibers are: (i) internal fibrillation—delaminating, loosening, and swelling of fiber wall; (ii) external fibrillation—peeling of fibrils from the fiber surface while remaining attached; (iii) fiber shortening—fiber cutting due to shearing action, and (iv) fines formation—primary fines come from ray cells and parenchyma cells and microfibrils that are caused by fiber shortening or external fibrillation. Moreover, the PFI refining could be adopted to obtain a higher internal fibrillation than other laboratory refiners [1]. These efects of the PFI refining on cellulosic fibers will improve the accessibility, the swelling, the flexibility, and the inter-fiber bonding capacity of fibers.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 1. Introduction\n[原文]\n It is assumed that these changes in the macro-level structure and properties are related to the changes of crystallinity and H-bonding network during refining [7,8].\n\nThere are some diferent conclusions regarding to the efects of PFI refining on crystallinity of cellulose, not like that of ball milling, which efectively reduces the crystallinity as the treatment progresses. Although some researchers considered that the crystallinity decreased during PFI refining for corn stover [9] or softwood pulp [10], some researchers reported that the crystallinity increased first and then decreased with the degree of refining for hardwood bleached kraft pulp fibers [11] or for unbleached eucalyptus fibers [12]. Moreover, Zhao et al. [7] reported that the crystallinity initially fluctuated upward and then downward, followed by a repeating fluctuation with PFI refining for tobacco stem mechanical pulp. None of the previous studies identified a clear trend, but the results were that the crystallinity varied during PFI refinement. Based on the large proportion of H-bonds in crystalline region of cellulose, it can be assumed that the H-bonding network might change during PFI refining.",

      "[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 3. Results and Discussions > 3.2. Effect of PFI Refining on Crystalline Index and Crystallite Size\n[原文]\nThe trends of CI (CI-XI and CI-XA) for softwood fibers and hardwood fibers were all similar, decreasing first and then increasing, along with a decline, as shown in Figure 4. The fluctuation of the CI was probably because of the mechanical action of PFI refining on the diferent regions of cellulose. In the first refining stage, the decrease of the CI showed that mechanical treatment may mainly act in the crystalline region. Subsequently, the growth of the CI could be interpreted as greater force acting on the amorphous region in which cocrystallization might occur upon drying under the mechanical and thermal action of PFI refining. The subsequent decrease might be the continuous destruction of crystalline region.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 3. Results and Discussions > 3.2. Effect of PFI Refining on Crystalline Index and Crystallite Size\n[原文]\nRecently, researches indicated that plant cell walls commonly contained microfibrils with 18 cellulose chains [26]. Frequently adopted arrangements of the 18 cellulose chains are 234432, 34443, and 333333 [27]. Therein, 234432 arrangement was found to be more probable based on calculation [28]. Thus, according to the crystallite sizes (as Table 1 shows) and the unit cell parameters of cellulose Iβ, there was most likely to be an average of two-fibrils with an arrangement of 234,432 packed side-by-side for both softwood fibers and hardwood fibers (as seen in Figure 5, drawn with mercury",
      "[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 3. Results and Discussions > 3.3. Efect of PFI Refining on H-Bonding Energies, H-Bonding Distances, and Content of H-Bonds\n[原文]\nFor the content of O(6)H···O(3′) inter-molecular H-bonds of softwood fiber, the trend can be divided into two stages, as shown in Table 2a. It decreased by 7.72% from 28.23% to 26.05% as refining from 0r to 4000 r and then increased by 9.14% from 4000 r to 8000 r, followed by a decrease of 17.13%, with the revolutions increasing from 8000 r to 16,000 r. Regarding the O(6)H···O(3′) H-bonds of hardwood fiber, the trend was almost similar to that of softwood fibers, except for a small increase of 0.45% from 8000 r to 12,000 r (in Table 2b). On the whole, the amount of the O(6)H···O(3′) H-bonds for softwood fibers and hardwood fibers decreased by 16.54% and 5.91% altogether, respectively. The decrease might be due to the cleavage among cellulose molecular chains under the mechanical action of PFI refining, which was closely related to internal and external fibrillation (as seen in Section 3.1). On the other hand, the increase illustrates that there was not only the breakage, but also the formation of O(6)H···O(3′) H-bonds.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 3. Results and Discussions > 3.3. Efect of PFI Refining on H-Bonding Energies, H-Bonding Distances, and Content of H-Bonds\n[原文]\n Both the fewer inter-molecular H-bonds and the lower CI (as Section 3.2 shows) will further improve the flexibility of cellulosic fibers, due to the higher mobility of molecular chains, the accessibility, and the WRV of fibers (as seen in Section 3.1).",
      "[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 3. Results and Discussions > 3.2. Effect of PFI Refining on Crystalline Index and Crystallite Size\n[原文]\nThe cellulose polymorph of these two fibers had no change during PFI treatment, which illustrates that the PFI refining is a relatively mild mechanical treatment, as the results of XRD in Online Resource (Figures S1 and S2) show. In general, the CI-XI and the CI-XA of softwood fibers showed a reduction of 4.66% and 15.47%, respectively, and those of hardwood fibers decreased by 2.65% and 19.4%, respectively, as can be seen in Figure 4 and Table 1. The value of the CI-XI was remarkably higher than the CI-XA, which might be caused by the over-fitting of amorphous contribution in the analysis of CI-XA. However, the CI-XI and the CI-XA were correlated significantly for both softwood fibers and hardwood fibers, with a correlation coefficient of 0.919 (p < 0.05) for softwood fibers and 0.925 (p < 0.05) for hardwood fibers, respectively, which is consistent with the report of Ahvenainen et al. [25].",

解析修复95块 · 要点 2/2；边界 2/2

PFI打浆过程中，两种纤维垂直于(200)晶面的晶粒尺寸总体呈上升趋势。 [1]
针叶浆纤维从不打浆到16000转，垂直于(200)晶面的晶粒尺寸依次为4.5、4.6、4.6、4.7、4.7 nm。 [6]
阔叶浆纤维从不打浆到16000转，垂直于(200)晶面的晶粒尺寸依次为4.5、4.7、4.8、4.8、4.7 nm。 [6]

      "[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 1. Introduction\n[原文]\nThere is still a lack of literature on the efects of PFI refinement on the H-bonding network. Particularly, the relationship between the content of H-bonds and crystallinity is still worthy of further study, which will deepen the understanding of the molecular aggregation and distribution of H-bonds, providing a molecular-scale explanation for the variations in accessibility, swelling, flexibility, and fibrillation of cellulosic fibers during PFI refinement. Therefore, this work explored the efects of PFI refinement on the CI, crystallite size, energy of H-bonds, H-bonding distance, and content of H-bonds for softwood pulp fibers and hardwood pulp fibers. Attempts were made in order to establish the correlations between the CI and content of various H-bonds.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 2. Methods > 2.1. PFI Refining\n[原文]\nCommercial bleached softwood and hardwood kraft pulp fibers were obtained from Zhongzhirenhe Company (Jinan, Shandong Province, China). Two pulp were treated with a PFI refiner (Hamjern Maskin A/S, Hamar, Norway) according to Tappi T248 wd-97, with a pulp consistency of 10%, the gap between the opposite refining plates was 0.2 mm, and forces per bar length were 3.33 N/mm and 1.77 N/mm for softwood fibers and hardwood fibers, respectively. The drainability was characterized by the Schopper Riegler number (SR-number) with the standards ISO 5267-1. Two pulp fibers were separately refined in a PFI refiner at 0, 4000, 8000, 12,000, and 16,000 revolutions and at 0, 4000, 8000, 12,000, and 16,000 revolutions, respectively. Corresponding various pulps with an increasing beating degree, such as 16, 20, 40, 63, and 79<sup>◦</sup> SR, were obtained for softwood fibers and 0, 26, 40, 57, and 70<sup>◦</sup> SR were obtained for hardwood fibers.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 2. Methods > 2.2. Morphological Analysis of Fibers and Mechanical Properties of Sheets\n[原文]\nThe fines content, weighted mean length, and macro-fibrillation index of each sample were determined with a MORFI LB analyzer (Techpap SAS, Grenoble, France). The tensile strength of dry sheets and Wet-web strength were tested according to TAPPI T494 and Chinese standard GBT 12914-2008, respectively. The zero-span tensile strength was tested with the Z-Span 2400 apparatus (Pulmac International Co. Ltd., Montpelier, VT, USA), according to the standard ISO 15361.",
      "[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 3. Results and Discussions > 3.1. The Morphological Analysis, Swelling, and Mechanical Properties\n[原文]\nFigure 1. The Morphological Analysis, Swelling, and Mechanical Properties\n[原文]\nThe beating degree and the WRV had a significant increment with increasing PFI refining revolutions, as can be seen in Figure 2. It is caused by the higher fibrillation that produces the new surface and more pores (as shown in Table S1 in Online Resource). The increase in swelling characterized by WRV makes the fibers more compliant in transverse [1], which contributes to improving the inter-fiber bonding strength of the fiber network. The results of fiber morphology analysis and water retention value showing that the fibrillation and the separation between fibrils increase with the refining process.",
      "[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 1. Introduction\n[原文]\nMechanical, chemical, and biological treatments are usually adopted to obtain the desired physical and mechanical properties and for further utilization of the natural cellulosic fibers. Therein, Papirindustriens forskningsinstitut (PFI) refining is the most common laboratory refiner in order to improve the inter-fiber bonding capacity [1] and accessibility [2,3], and manufacture the micro-fibrillated or nano-fibrillated cellulose [4–6]. The main efects of PFI refining on fibers are: (i) internal fibrillation—delaminating, loosening, and swelling of fiber wall; (ii) external fibrillation—peeling of fibrils from the fiber surface while remaining attached; (iii) fiber shortening—fiber cutting due to shearing action, and (iv) fines formation—primary fines come from ray cells and parenchyma cells and microfibrils that are caused by fiber shortening or external fibrillation. Moreover, the PFI refining could be adopted to obtain a higher internal fibrillation than other laboratory refiners [1]. These efects of the PFI refining on cellulosic fibers will improve the accessibility, the swelling, the flexibility, and the inter-fiber bonding capacity of fibers.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 1. Introduction\n[原文]\n It is assumed that these changes in the macro-level structure and properties are related to the changes of crystallinity and H-bonding network during refining [7,8].\n\nThere are some diferent conclusions regarding to the efects of PFI refining on crystallinity of cellulose, not like that of ball milling, which efectively reduces the crystallinity as the treatment progresses. Although some researchers considered that the crystallinity decreased during PFI refining for corn stover [9] or softwood pulp [10], some researchers reported that the crystallinity increased first and then decreased with the degree of refining for hardwood bleached kraft pulp fibers [11] or for unbleached eucalyptus fibers [12]. Moreover, Zhao et al. [7] reported that the crystallinity initially fluctuated upward and then downward, followed by a repeating fluctuation with PFI refining for tobacco stem mechanical pulp. None of the previous studies identified a clear trend, but the results were that the crystallinity varied during PFI refinement. Based on the large proportion of H-bonds in crystalline region of cellulose, it can be assumed that the H-bonding network might change during PFI refining.",
      "[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 3. Results and Discussions > 3.2. Effect of PFI Refining on Crystalline Index and Crystallite Size\n[原文]\nThe trends of CI (CI-XI and CI-XA) for softwood fibers and hardwood fibers were all similar, decreasing first and then increasing, along with a decline, as shown in Figure 4. The fluctuation of the CI was probably because of the mechanical action of PFI refining on the diferent regions of cellulose. In the first refining stage, the decrease of the CI showed that mechanical treatment may mainly act in the crystalline region. Subsequently, the growth of the CI could be interpreted as greater force acting on the amorphous region in which cocrystallization might occur upon drying under the mechanical and thermal action of PFI refining. The subsequent decrease might be the continuous destruction of crystalline region.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 3. Results and Discussions > 3.2. Effect of PFI Refining on Crystalline Index and Crystallite Size\n[原文]\nRecently, researches indicated that plant cell walls commonly contained microfibrils with 18 cellulose chains [26]. Frequently adopted arrangements of the 18 cellulose chains are 234432, 34443, and 333333 [27]. Therein, 234432 arrangement was found to be more probable based on calculation [28]. Efect of PFI Refining on H-Bonding Energies, H-Bonding Distances, and Content of H-Bonds\n[原文]\nFor the content of O(6)H···O(3′) inter-molecular H-bonds of softwood fiber, the trend can be divided into two stages, as shown in Table 2a. It decreased by 7.72% from 28.23% to 26.05% as refining from 0r to 4000 r and then increased by 9.14% from 4000 r to 8000 r, followed by a decrease of 17.13%, with the revolutions increasing from 8000 r to 16,000 r. Regarding the O(6)H···O(3′) H-bonds of hardwood fiber, the trend was almost similar to that of softwood fibers, except for a small increase of 0.45% from 8000 r to 12,000 r (in Table 2b). On the whole, the amount of the O(6)H···O(3′) H-bonds for softwood fibers and hardwood fibers decreased by 16.54% and 5.91% altogether, respectively. The decrease might be due to the cleavage among cellulose molecular chains under the mechanical action of PFI refining, which was closely related to internal and external fibrillation (as seen in Section 3.1). On the other hand, the increase illustrates that there was not only the breakage, but also the formation of O(6)H···O(3′) H-bonds.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 3. Results and Discussions > 3.3. Efect of PFI Refining on H-Bonding Energies, H-Bonding Distances, and Content of H-Bonds\n[原文]\n Both the fewer inter-molecular H-bonds and the lower CI (as Section 3.2 shows) will further improve the flexibility of cellulosic fibers, due to the higher mobility of molecular chains, the accessibility, and the WRV of fibers (as seen in Section 3.1)."

The increase in swelling\ncharacterized by WRV makes the ﬁbers more compliant in transverse [1], which contributes to\nimproving the inter-ﬁber bonding strength of the ﬁber network. [7] reported that the crystallinity initially\nﬂuctuated upward and then downward, followed by a repeating ﬂuctuation with PFI reﬁning for\ntobacco stem mechanical pulp. None of the previous studies identiﬁed a clear trend, but the results\nwere that the crystallinity varied during PFI reﬁnement. Based on the large proportion of H-bonds in\ncrystalline region of cellulose, it can be assumed that the H-bonding network might change during\nPFI reﬁning.\nFourier transformation infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR), which is sensitive to molecular structure,\ncan be as an indirect measurement for studying H-bonding network. FT-IR deconvolution of hydroxyl\ngroups band was adopted in order to study the changes of the energy of H-bonds and the H-bonding\ndistance during deligniﬁcation [13] or the deconstruction of cellulose [14]. Moreover, it was used\nto study the diﬀerences of the content of H-bonds not only between dislocation region and normal\nregion [15], but also among plant species [16,17]. Regarding the changes of H-bonding network during\nPFI reﬁning, Yuan et al. [18] reported that the content of H-bonds and crystallinity index (CI) of\neucalyptus ﬁbers changed with the increment of beating time. Subsequently, Zhao et al. [8] found that\nthe H-bonding energy for O(6)H· · · O(3′) inter-molecular H-bonds decreased by 12.9% and evolutions\nof the content of certain H-bonds diﬀered at various reﬁning stages.\n\nThere is still a lack of literature on the eﬀects of PFI reﬁnement on the H-bonding network.\nParticularly, the relationship between the content of H-bonds and crystallinity is still worthy of\nfurther study, which will deepen the understanding of the molecular aggregation and distribution of\nH-bonds, providing a molecular-scale explanation for the variations in accessibility, swelling, ﬂexibility,\nand ﬁbrillation of cellulosic ﬁbers during PFI reﬁnement. Therefore, this work explored the eﬀects\nof PFI reﬁnement on the CI, crystallite size, energy of H-bonds, H-bonding distance, and content of\nH-bonds for softwood pulp ﬁbers and hardwood pulp ﬁbers. In addition, it is noticeable that the (110)\nplanes possess the highest theoretical roughness and accessibility to the hydrophilic groups in cellulose\nIβ [28]. Throughout the reﬁning of two pulp ﬁbers, the sizes perpendicular to (110) plane were more\nvolatile than the (110) plane and (200) plane, which is consistent with the report of Duchemin et al.,\nas shown in Table 1a,b [29]. It could be interpreted to be that water molecules were easier to permeate\nthrough the spaces between the hydrophilic (110) planes in paracrystalline region (hydration), and then\nit made these planes suﬀer more mechanical actions, so there was more adhesion (cocrystallization)\nand cleavage of cellulose chains created for (110) plane during PFI reﬁning.\nHowever, the crystallite size that was perpendicular to (200) lattice plane of two ﬁbers had an\nupward trend during PFI reﬁning. PFI2-011 · 是不是打浆转数越高，纤维素结晶度就越低？

参考答案与评分要点

不是单调下降。针叶木CI-XI从4000转70.42%升到8000转72.54%；阔叶木也从73.01%升到75.06%。0转到16000转总体下降，但过程中先降、回升、再降。

表格行检索＋关联补全 · 要点 0.5/2；边界 1/2

不能简单判定打浆转数越高结晶度越低；关于PFI精磨对纤维素结晶度的影响，既有研究报道过下降、先升高后降低以及反复波动等不同结果，且未识别出明确趋势。 [2]
该研究的结论指出，总体而言微晶尺寸、结晶度和各类氢键含量变化不大，PFI精磨主要是纤颤化处理，对超分子结构破坏相对较小。 [3]
因此，根据所给证据，打浆转数与纤维素结晶度之间不存在明确的“转数越高结晶度越低”的单调关系。 [2] [3]

      "text": "[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 1. Introduction\n[原文]\nMechanical, chemical, and biological treatments are usually adopted to obtain the desired physical and mechanical properties and for further utilization of the natural cellulosic fibers. Therein, Papirindustriens forskningsinstitut (PFI) refining is the most common laboratory refiner in order to improve the inter-fiber bonding capacity [1] and accessibility [2,3], and manufacture the micro-fibrillated or nano-fibrillated cellulose [4–6]. The main efects of PFI refining on fibers are: (i) internal fibrillation—delaminating, loosening, and swelling of fiber wall; (ii) external fibrillation—peeling of fibrils from the fiber surface while remaining attached; (iii) fiber shortening—fiber cutting due to shearing action, and (iv) fines formation—primary fines come from ray cells and parenchyma cells and microfibrils that are caused by fiber shortening or external fibrillation. Moreover, the PFI refining could be adopted to obtain a higher internal fibrillation than other laboratory refiners [1]. These efects of the PFI refining on cellulosic fibers will improve the accessibility, the swelling, the flexibility, and the inter-fiber bonding capacity of fibers.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 1. Introduction\n[原文]\n It is assumed that these changes in the macro-level structure and properties are related to the changes of crystallinity and H-bonding network during refining [7,8].\n\nThere are some diferent conclusions regarding to the efects of PFI refining on crystallinity of cellulose, not like that of ball milling, which efectively reduces the crystallinity as the treatment progresses. Although some researchers considered that the crystallinity decreased during PFI refining for corn stover [9] or softwood pulp [10], some researchers reported that the crystallinity increased first and then decreased with the degree of refining for hardwood bleached kraft pulp fibers [11] or for unbleached eucalyptus fibers [12]. Moreover, Zhao et al. [7] reported that the crystallinity initially fluctuated upward and then downward, followed by a repeating fluctuation with PFI refining for tobacco stem mechanical pulp. None of the previous studies identified a clear trend, but the results were that the crystallinity varied during PFI refinement. Based on the large proportion of H-bonds in crystalline region of cellulose, it can be assumed that the H-bonding network might change during PFI refining.",
